title: When is Warmstarting Effective for Scaling Language Models?

paper.title: When is Warmstarting Effective for Scaling Language Models?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Model growth from a given checkpoint aims to accelerate training of a larger model, offering potential resource savings.
Despite recent interest, warmstarting has seen limited practical adoption in large-scale training.
We attribute this to two underexplored factors: (1) an overemphasis on preserving the smaller model’s performance at initialization, which constrains operator design for new architectures, and (2) insufficient analysis of how growth interacts with hyperparameters and scaling behavior, compounded by inconsistent growth factors across the literature. We show that preserving the base model’s initial post-growth performance is not necessary for strong final performance, and that simple, architecture-agnostic growth strategies can outperform more complex warmstarting operators.
Crucially, we empirically identify an upper bound on the growth factor g g beyond which training from scratch is more efficient.
We observe this across multiple ablation setups.
Notably, this limit is also present, but unreported, in prior published results.
Across our experiments on dense MLPs and dense language models, we find that a 2 × 2\times growth factor is the most reliable in yielding convergence speedups, with gains most pronounced under 20 tokens/parameter budgets and diminishing as budget increases.
We fit scaling laws over these observations to provide predictive guidance for practitioners deciding when and how much to grow.
Together, our analysis provides practical guidelines and empirical limits for model growth.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Training state-of-the-art deep learning models requires significant computational resources. As models scale from millions to billions of parameters, practitioners face an important question: can we reuse the compute invested in training smaller models when scaling up? Model growth or warmstarting ( WS ), i.e., initializing larger models from trained smaller checkpoints, offers potential efficiency gains, yet remains largely absent from production pipelines despite substantial research ( Gong et al., 2019 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Rae et al., 2021 ; Shen et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023a ; Wang et al., 2023b ; Deng et al., 2023 ; Samragh et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Deep Learning (DL) success has been built on pushing the loss frontier across tasks, applications, and data modalities ( Krizhevsky et al., 2012 ; He et al., 2016 ; Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Brown et al., 2020 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; OpenAI, 2024 ) . As training efficacy improves, processing larger datasets drives corresponding increases in model capacity ( Alabdulmohsin et al., 2023 ) . Current research on frontier models builds on seminal scaling law studies demonstrating the necessity of simultaneously growing both model size and data processed ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . This co-scaling question continues to evolve across different constraints, modalities, and architectures, with the traditional goal of pushing the loss-frontier now complemented by optimizing the compute-optimal frontier ( Anagnostidis et al., 2024 ) . In practice, these considerations translate to decisions about resource efficiency ( Wan et al., 2023 ) . While WS has been periodically explored across architectures and paradigms, it has not become standard practice in training pipelines, often remaining an academic topic rather than a common choice in DL pipelines ( Gong et al., 2019 ; Wang et al., 2023a ) . We identify three barriers to practical WS adoption: 1) Implementation complexity: existing methods require architecture-specific adaptations and may not generalize to modern components ( Su et al., 2021 ; Gu and Dao, 2023 ) ; 2) Unclear growth limits: practitioners lack guidance on how much a given checkpoint can be grown before WS becomes counterproductive ( Xie et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023a ) ; 3) Hyperparameter opacity under scaling: the interaction between WS methods, hyperparameters, and model and data scaling budgets is under-explored, creating tuning overhead that undermines efficiency gains ( Fetterman et al., 2023 ; Dey et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, in scaling regimes where both models and data grow to improve final convergence loss, measuring relative early-stage convergence speed may not adequately capture practical requirements ( Shin et al., 2024 ; Unlu, 2026 ) . In this work, we attempt to systematically investigate when WS is truly effective, in a first-principles manner, to address these barriers. We limit the discussion scope, both for clarity and computation, for the case when a base model checkpoint is available to be WS -ed to a larger model scale. We assume that we are aware of the dataset the base was trained on, and that some of its training hyperparameters may be available, but we treat it as a black-box when it comes to the training compute invested in it (unlike the assumption made by Liew and Kato (2025) ). We believe this better reflects a real-world scenario where only model checkpoints are publicly released. Our contributions are: 1. We generalize warmstarting growth into shrink-zero-perturb ( SZP ), a simple architecture-agnostic operation, and find that exact function-preservation is not required for effective warmstarting. 2. We empirically establish an upper bound on the growth ratio of a given checkpoint, such that, beyond this bound, training the grown model from scratch converges as fast as warmstarting it. 3. Using scaling-law fits, we show that for a given warmstarting method and base model size, the convergence advantage over training from scratch persists only within a bounded token budget, and we predict where this crossover occurs. The paper proceeds as follows: Section 2 reviews prior warmstarting methods and guidance; Section 3 introduces SZP and its design motivation; Section 4 reports hyperparameter transfer, growth limits, and scaling-law predictions; and Section 5 summarizes practical guidelines and limitations. We release our model and training pipelines in the linked repository 1 1 1 https://github.com/Neeratyoy/warmstarting_exps .

sections.heading: 2 Related Works
sections.text: Model growth as initialization is the broad class of WS techniques that derive the weights of a larger model from a smaller, typically well-trained checkpoint, before beginning training. Here, the aim is to transfer the knowledge learned by the smaller model to improve the larger model’s training efficiency. Net2Net ( Chen et al., 2016 ) and Network Morphisms ( Wei et al., 2016 ) are among the earliest works exploring model growth for Deep Learning. At the time, the scope was limited to convolutional networks, but the core idea was carried forward to evolving architectures ( Gong et al., 2019 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Samragh et al., 2024 ) . The benefit lies in being a one-time operation before training, requiring only weights from a smaller network of the same architectural family. A central idea in designing WS operations for initialization is that of function-preservation ( FP ), wherein the grown model’s output at the first forward pass matches that of the base model checkpoint used for WS . Introduced by Chen et al. (2016) for Deep Learning, FP has dominated the width-scaling WS paradigm ( Wang et al., 2023b ; Samragh et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . However, with new architectures, it typically requires special adaptation to remain function preserving ( Chen et al., 2021 ; Samragh et al., 2024 ) . We thus question if FP at initialization is a requirement for model growth. Karp et al. (2024) already showed that loss after a short training budget correlates better than loss at initialization with growth operator rankings. We extend this to more practical training budgets. Learned model growth is the other family of WS that does not fix the exact manner of WS operation but handles it dynamically. Wang et al. (2023a) introduces a Kronecker-factored linear operator that parameterizes the linear map from the small to the larger model, learned over a few steps of training (in the style of Karp et al. (2024) ). Here, the Kronecker product constrains growth ratios but works for both width and depth. Evci et al. (2022) looks at dynamic model growing during training by maximizing the gradient norms of the newly added neurons to enforce faster convergence, while the output-preservation in the function-preservation -style is still implied. The learned component here comes from the newly grown weights set through SVD over the gradient on the activations. This design looks to prevent dead neurons in grown models, which can lead to early rank collapse or not utilize the grown parameter capacity and move sufficiently away in the function hypothesis space from the base model. This connects to plasticity loss ( Lyle et al., 2023 ) , which correlates with dead (inactive) neurons, low effective rank representations, and growing weight magnitudes. Dohare et al. (2023) addresses this for a trained model by selectively reinitializing a fraction of low-utility neurons, scored by their activations, after each training step to keep a model in a continual learning setup. In this work, we focus entirely on the more straightforward setup of initialization-only WS . Full-state Warmstarting looks beyond the weights. Wang et al. (2024) looks at the learning rate schedulers, Ma et al. (2026) and Yu et al. (2026) necessitate the WS of optimizer states too. These families aim to preserve loss (and thereby FP ), while suitably inducing training dynamics through optimizer schedules and states, including hyperparameters. Our setup assumes that only the smaller model checkpoint is available and no other information on the optimizer or scheduler, especially their states. The framework of investigation we offer in our paper should apply to future studies extending to complete training state warmstarts, too. Warmstarting in practical settings has been covered mostly in terms of operator selection ( Karp et al., 2024 ) , for scaling related recommendations involving scaling laws ( Wang et al., 2023b ; Liew and Kato, 2025 ) , and the role of width-depth in WS efficacy ( Du et al., 2024 ) . We note that most WS literature varies in their setups, especially with respect to growth factors g g (the ratio of target to base model parameters) and the budget involved in training. Our investigation in this work focuses specifically on width-scaling strategies. Typically, joint scaling of models along both dimensions requires independent choice of width- and depth-growth operators ( Du et al., 2024 ) . Our study here is compatible with any depth-growing and thereby joint-growing setups. We adopt a “black-box” assumption where the tokens spent on the base checkpoint are unknown, and we are concerned primarily with the question of how much we can grow this model, by training for how much budget, to ensure there is a benefit over training from scratch. In the remaining paper, we treat the terms Model Growth and Warmstarting ( WS ) synonymously. Refer to Appendix A for additional literature on hyperparameter transfer and scaling laws.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: This section defines the WS ( Warmstarting ) setup for our empirical study ( Section 4 ). We first introduce a compact design space for growth ( Section 3.1 ) that abstracts common warmstarting operators. We then use this space to identify a robust, architecture-agnostic default in SZP ( Section 3.2 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Design Space for Warmstarting
sections.text: To study when Warmstarting is effective, we compare simple, architecture-agnostic WS operations against training from scratch. Function-preservation ( FP ) methods typically combine three ingredients: cloning existing weights, scaling grown weights, and adding noise, often through architecture-specific rules ( Chen et al., 2016 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Samragh et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) (see Appendix G ). We instead keep these interacting design choices independent and apply them uniformly across all components, both 1 1 D and 2 2 D weights. We define our design space by extending the shrink-and-perturb ( SnP ) formulation from Continual Learning (CL) ( Ash and Adams, 2020 ) . In its original form, target weights θ target \theta_{\text{target}} are derived by rescaling the base weights and adding Gaussian noise: θ target l = λ shrink ⋅ θ base l + 𝒩 ( 0 , σ perturb ) 2 \theta_{\text{target}}^{l}~=~\lambda_{\text{shrink}}{}\cdot\theta_{\text{base}}^{l}+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\text{perturb}}{}^{2}) (1) where λ shrink \lambda_{\text{shrink}}{} regulates the influence of inherited weights and σ perturb \sigma_{\text{perturb}}{} controls the standard deviation of Gaussian noise, used as perturbation for all neurons. To adapt this for model growth, where the target model is larger than the base, we augment (in blue ) the formulation with a growth function, 𝒢 \mathcal{G} : θ target l = λ shrink ⋅ 𝒢 ⁡ ( θ base l , p , q ) ¯ + 𝒩 ( 0 , σ perturb ) 2 , \theta_{\text{target}}^{l}~=~\lambda_{\text{shrink}}{}\cdot\underline{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{G}(\theta_{\text{base}}^{l},p,q)}+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\text{perturb}}{}^{2}), (2) where 𝒢 : ℝ m × n × ℕ × ℕ → ℝ p × q \mathcal{G}{}:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\times\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\rightarrow{}\mathbb{R}^{p\times q} maps the base weights θ base l ∈ ℝ m × n \theta_{\text{base}}^{l}~\in~\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} into the larger target shape p × q p\times q ( p ≥ m , q ≥ n p\geq m,q\geq n ). Here, λ shrink ∈ ℛ > 0 \lambda_{\text{shrink}}{}\in\mathcal{R}>0 and σ perturb ∈ ℛ \sigma_{\text{perturb}}{}\in\mathcal{R} , and l ∈ 𝒩 l\in\mathcal{N} denoting layer index.

sections.heading: Intuition and Motivation.
sections.text: By separating 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , λ shrink \lambda_{\text{shrink}}{} , and σ perturb \sigma_{\text{perturb}}{} in a WS operations, it gives a lightweight abstraction of common FP -style operations without requiring component-specific rules for exact function preservation. Formally, Equation 2 can represent more complex operators like Net2Net through appropriate choices of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , λ shrink \lambda_{\text{shrink}}{} , and σ perturb \sigma_{\text{perturb}}{} , per architecture component ( Samragh et al., 2024 ) , though deriving such mappings remains intentionally out of scope here. Conceptually, Growth determines which structure is inherited from the base model. Perturbation is critical for symmetry breaking, that is, it ensures that newly added neurons can learn distinct features rather than simply duplicating inherited behavior. Finally, Shrinking reduces the magnitude of inherited weights, dampening the dominance of base representations, and allows the new neurons to participate meaningfully in learning. Together, these axes yield simple WS realizations that connect cleanly to established CL concepts while remaining easy to implement. We offer theoretical intuition in Appendix C.1 and perform a mechanistic analysis of this setup in Appendix C.2 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Choosing a Default Warmstarting Method
sections.text: Figure 1: Comparing the simplest set of realizations of Equation 2 , for different target scale runs, given the base checkpoint; Zeros and Clone represent the choices for 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , the growth function; 𝒢 + \mathcal{G}{}+ Perturb represents λ shrink = 1 \lambda_{\text{shrink}}{}=1 , or no shrinking; SnP - 𝒢 \mathcal{G}{} represents λ shrink = 1 \lambda_{\text{shrink}}{}=1 ; For each choice of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , we observe: SnP - 𝒢 ≥ 𝒢 + Perturb ≥ 𝒢 \mathcal{G}{}~\geq~\mathcal{G}{}+\text{Perturb}~\geq~\mathcal{G} , in terms of convergence rates. SnP represents Equation 1 and SnP - 𝒢 \mathcal{G}{} represents Equation 2 . We compare representative realizations of the design space in Figure 1 to select a robust default for our scaling experiments. In Figure 1 , Zeros and Clone show no significant difference in isolation, but each improves with perturbation noise ( Zeros+Perturb , Clone+Perturb ), and further with shrinking ( Shrink+Zeros+Perturb , Shrink+Clone+Perturb ) across growth ratios. We view these variants as streamlined realizations of WS that remain architecture-agnostic and easy to implement. A function-preservation analogue would instead set the scaling magnitude relative to grown sizes, apply a weight-type-specific cloning operation, and similarly adjust the perturbation magnitude ( Chen et al., 2016 ; Samragh et al., 2024 ) . Notably, all WS variants recover the base-model loss within a few steps and converge faster than Scratch early in training. However, the differences between variants become clearer in sustained convergence, where SZP ( Shrink+Zeros+Perturb ) is the only variant consistently superior across model widths. We therefore use SZP as our main architecture-agnostic WS method. While simplicity is subjective, SZP strikes a practical middle ground: it mirrors the structure of standard FP algorithms while loosening the strict constraint of preserving base-model outputs at initialization. We emphasize that SZP is not proposed as a new state-of-the-art warmstarting algorithm, but as a principled baseline we find effective for studying the scaling behavior of WS in Section 4 .

sections.heading: 4 Empirical Study
sections.text: In this section, we use the SZP setup to study its scaling behavior, compare against popular function-preservation baselines such as Net2Net , observe the existence of an upper bound on the growth factor, and fit scaling laws to characterize when training from scratch outperforms Warmstarting ( WS ). We distill these findings into practical recommendations.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experiment Setup
sections.text: Following Qiu et al. (2025) , we use the synthetic regression task as a controlled testbed for scaling and WS (refer to Appendix B for more details). This setting is computationally light to afford dense hyperparameter sweeps at both base and target widths, for all run types: Scratch , and WS runs ( Net2Net and SZP ). The language modeling setup, used for the broader empirical comparison, is described below. We report the corresponding compute estimates in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 4.1.1 Hyperparameter Selection
sections.text: When treating WS as an initialization, it is expected to reshape the loss landscape over hyperparameters. Prior comparisons of WS operations have under-explored this. This matters particularly when WS to much larger models, where re-tuning costs can be prohibitive. Here, we use the synthetic MLP regression task to compare tuning strategies across WS operations.

sections.heading: Training Hyperparameters.
sections.text: The tuned hyperparameters are detailed in Table 2 and summarized in Figure 2 , where violins show the final validation loss distribution from a dense grid search at each target width for Scratch , Net2Net , and SZP . For transfer, we take the best configuration at the base width of 48 48 and transfer it as (1) unchanged ( static transfer ), or (2) with width-aware μ ​ P \mu\text{P} scaling rules ( Yang et al., 2021 ) . We refer readers to Appendix B.4 for background and details on μ ​ P \mu\text{P} . Figure 2: Final validation loss under MLP-width scaling from a fixed base width of 48 48 . For each target width, each triplet of violins shows Scratch, Net2Net , and SZP from left to right. Violins summarize the final-loss distribution over a dense target-scale hyperparameter grid (Appendix, Table 2 ); horizontal ticks denote the median and minimum losses within each grid. Open circles mark static transfer : the best base-width hyperparameters unchanged at the target width. Stars mark width-aware transfer : the base-width optimum follows μ ​ P \mu\text{P}{} scaling rules (Appendix B.5 ). Figure 2 shows that dense tuning at the target width usually yields the best configuration when the budget allows. The effectiveness of transfer, however, depends on the initialization method. Static transfer worsens with growth factor for both Scratch and SZP , while Net2Net ’s function-preservation aspect makes it more robust. Crucially, μ ​ P \mu\text{P} transfer is consistently near-optimal relative to the dense grid and outperforms static transfer across all run types. This motivates us to use μ ​ P \mu\text{P}{} transfer for all subsequent compute-heavy experiments, especially the language model runs reported in later sections. Notably, the best attainable losses across dense grid search over Scratch , Net2Net , and SZP converge as the growth factor increases. This hints at the practical limits of WS that we examine more closely in Section 4.2 .

sections.heading: SZP Design Choices.
sections.text: In function-preservation -based methods, the perturbation noise and scaling applied to base or new neurons depend on the architectural component. We instead apply Equation 2 uniformly across all weights and thus fix the scaling variable and the perturbation noise form. For perturbation noise, we use the scale-dependent σ perturb = 1 / width \sigma_{\mathrm{perturb}}=1/\sqrt{\mathrm{width}} applied under both Static transfer and μ \mu P. This choice is common in Deep Learning and has also been used in FP -based setups ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . We provide an ablation on the perturbation noise in Appendix C.3 , where we observe that the noise scale affects the convergence rate more than the final generalization loss. Just as perturbation is essential for new neurons to break symmetry inherited from the base model and use the full target capacity ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , shrinking is essential for reducing weight norms, increasing effective ranks, and maintaining plasticity. We follow Ash and Adams (2020) and fix λ shrink = 0.4 \lambda_{\text{shrink}}{}=0.4 in our experiments to isolate the effect of other variables. Our ablation in Appendix C.4 confirms that λ shrink ∈ { 0.2 , 0.4 } \lambda_{\text{shrink}}{}\in\{0.2,~0.4\} offers improved performance over training from scratch for reasonable growth factors. We additionally provide a simple theoretical sketch in Appendix C.1 for why zero-padding, perturbation, and shrinkage play complementary roles.

sections.heading: 4.1.2 Language Model Setup
sections.text: All language-model experiments train decoder-only GPT-2 style models ( Radford et al., 2019 ) using the open-source LitGPT implementation ( LitGPT, 2023 ) on the SlimPajama corpus ( Soboleva et al., 2023 ) . We perform only width-scaling here, consistent with our scope of studying FP -based WS . All runs used AdamW and a warmup-stable-decay learning rate scheduler with warmup and cooldown lengths set to fixed fractions of the total training budget. Each run’s training budget is set to 10 , 20 , or ​ 30 10,~20,~\text{or}~30 tokens/parameter . We train models ranging from 14 14 M to 1.2 1.2 B parameters. Except for dense grid searches at multiple base scales, all Scratch and WS runs at scales larger than the base use μ ​ P \mu\text{P}{} transfer for learning rates, and we scale the base-scale optimal batch size. Additional training and hyperparameter details are provided in Appendix D . We additionally present ablations of SZP performance on the LLaMa architecture in Appendix F.1 .

sections.heading: 4.2 Practical Warmstarting
sections.text: In this section, we focus on language model experiments and address our primary question of how and where to find gains when Warmstarting . Top row : comparing Scratch to SZP up to 1.2 1.2 B parameters, showing that SZP converges faster and achieves better final loss, with gains varying across growth factors g g (rightmost). Bottom row : comparing Net2Net to SZP (both WS methods explored here) for up to 610 610 M parameters, showing that SZP consistently outperforms the FP -based baseline.

sections.heading: Empirical Performance of SZP .
sections.text: We report performance scaling for SZP up to 1.2 1.2 B parameters in Figure 3 (top), including downstream task performances in Appendix F.2 . Both rows show that SZP converges faster than Scratch and Net2Net . Most notably, the relative performance gains of the WS operations ( Net2Net and SZP ) diminish as the growth factor g g grows. Figure 3 (rightmost, both rows) shows all the learning curves trained for 10 , 20 , and ​ 30 10,~20,~\text{and}~30 tokens/parameter s, for different base-target pairings, with identical learning rate schedules, confirming that faster convergence holds across scales for both comparisons. The difference in final loss is more subtle and is discussed more in later sections, where we fit scaling laws and systematically characterize the regimes in which WS outperforms training from Scratch , and SZP outperforms Net2Net . The variance in performance difference across growth factors is a central observation of this work. The base model used to derive grown weights is typically well-trained, with its learned function occupying a subspace of the weight space, and exploiting this subspace is where WS ’s efficiency gains originate (signal preservation). For function-preservation methods, which typically rely on clone operations, this subspace can be hard to escape due to inherent symmetries in the grown weights ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . Figure 7 (right) (see, Appendix C.2 ) reflects this in the lower effective rank of Net2Net compared to SZP . Decomposing weight movement into radial (along the initialization) and angular (orthogonal) components, we find that SZP ’s attention layers show both rotation and scaling of the weights at initialization, while Net2Net ’s radial component remains much more stable and weight adjustment is dominated by rotations than scaling the initialization vector. The practical impact of this may show up in too well-trained base models saturating WS performance ( Liew and Kato, 2025 ) or growing a base checkpoint too large such that gains diminish. In the next section, we observe and discuss this in more detail. Figure 4: IsoFLOPs on Language Models and MLPs for 20 tokens/parameter . Blue lines (the line connecting the trough of the IsoFLOPs) mark the optimal growth factor, g opt g_{\text{opt}}{} , at each IsoFLOP line, while red lines (the vertical line right of the g opt g_{\text{opt}} line) mark the g upper g_{\text{upper}} , the upper bound on the growth factor at which WS matches the loss of training from Scratch ( g = 1 g=1 ). These lines are obtained from a quadratic fit to the validation loss rather than directly from the loss values. Additional results for more target sizes and budgets can be found in Appendix H.1 .

sections.heading: The Bounded Effective Growth Factor.
sections.text: For practitioners with a fixed base checkpoint seeking to scale up (as scoped in Section 1 ), a key question is how much the model can grow while preserving WS ’s efficiency gains over Scratch . Prior work ( Du et al., 2024 ) shows that WS performance depends on the growth factor g g , defined as the ratio of target to base model parameters, and characterizes this via the optimal growth factor. This optimal factor, which we term g opt g_{\text{opt}} , is estimated by fitting quadratic models to IsoFLOP losses and minimizing them. g opt g_{\text{opt}} is meant to be an optimal growth factor such that it maximizes the relative gains of WS over training from Scratch . We argue this optimization-based characterization is hard to support from sparse evaluations, since reliably identifying g opt g_{\text{opt}} requires substantially denser measurements, especially for g ∈ ( 1 , g opt ) g\in(1,g_{\text{opt}}{}) . Instead, we propose reporting g upper g_{\text{upper}} , which we observe as the largest growth factor under which WS still improves over Scratch ’s final validation loss. This can be extracted by drawing a horizontal line from g = 1 g=1 for each IsoFLOP line, cutting the parabola at a g > 1 g>1 . We posit that g upper g_{\text{upper}} offers a more flexible and practical recommendation for WS in practice, and assess relative gains of different WS operations. While such a bound is implicit in prior results Du et al. (2024) , it has not been reported as a quantity of interest. In Figure 4 , we reproduce these results for SZP and Net2Net in the LLM setting (MLP included as verification), modeling IsoFLOP lines with quadratic fits across growth factors ( g = 1 g=1 denotes Scratch ). Both g opt g_{\text{opt}} (blue) and g upper g_{\text{upper}} (red) are read off the fit. g upper g_{\text{upper}} is observed across all settings. The exception is Net2Net in the LLM setting, where g upper = 1 g_{\text{upper}}=1 (the Scratch run) at the final IsoFLOPs eventually beats Net2Net by the end of the scheduled budget (when including the learning rate decay). This is consistent with Du et al. (2024) 2 2 2 Du et al. (2024) reports that width-only scaling with FP underperforms, while their IsoFLOP analysis on growth factors for width-only scaling also exhibits a g upper g_{\text{upper}} bound. and highlights the shortcomings of function-preservation methods on more complex architectures (refer to Appendix G ). For complete IsoFLOPs results, refer to Appendix H.1 . One interpretation is that Warmstarting places the target model in a region of the loss landscape shaped by the base model’s learned representations. For small g g , this initialization provides a favorable basin for efficient convergence. As g g grows, the base model occupies a diminishing fraction of the target architecture, and the initialization increasingly resembles a random one. Beyond g upper g_{\text{upper}} , the constraints imposed by the inherited structure outweigh its benefits, anchoring the warmstarted model in a suboptimal region. Consistent with this, our mechanistic analysis ( Figure 13 ) shows that warmstarted models at higher g g increasingly resemble Scratch across interpretability metrics, suggesting gradual dilution of the base model’s structure. The stability of g upper g_{\text{upper}} across model scales further supports this. The rate at which warmstarted representations converge to Scratch -like behavior depends primarily on the architectural ratio g g , and not on absolute model size. In summary , we observe a bound on the effective growth factor g upper g_{\text{upper}} , consistent with Du et al. (2024) , and argue that identifying and reporting it is crucial for practical adoption of WS . When budget does not permit investigating g upper g_{\text{upper}} , we recommend g = 2 g=2 as a conservative default. Much of the WS literature restricts to 2 × 2\times growth ( Samragh et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) , leaving g upper g_{\text{upper}}{} undiscussed. For fair comparison of WS operations, g upper g_{\text{upper}}{} should be discussed and, where possible, investigated. Figure 5: Isolines for loss difference showing where Warmstarting achieves lower loss than training from Scratch for growth factor g ≈ 2 g\approx 2 (blue regions indicate Warmstarting is better; red indicates Scratch is better; the green line marks the boundary where both perform equally). Given a fixed model size, the more the tokens/parameter , the more preferred is training from Scratch over Warmstarting . The region where SZP is effective is larger than that of Net2Net, enabling a more complete comparison between growth methods.

sections.heading: Effective Warmstarting Across Scale.
sections.text: Scaling a language model involves growing both the model and the data budget. As discussed, diminishing gains are expected from WS , so studying its effectiveness at a single token budget and sparse model sizes provides only a limited, possibly misleading, signal. While Liew and Kato (2025) identified that overtraining base models diminishes WS gains, we highlight the effect of g upper g_{\text{upper}} on parameter scaling. Since we assume the base model’s training budget is unknown, we focus on the practical requirement of specifying the target budget. We subset our collected data for g ≈ 2 g\approx 2 ( Figure 4 ) and follow Approach 3 from Hoffmann et al. (2022) to fit the power-law parametric form predicting loss as a function of parameters N N and tokens D D , L ⁡ ( N , D ) = E + A N α + B D β , L(N,D)=E+\frac{A}{N^{\alpha}}+\frac{B}{D^{\beta}}, where E , A , α , B , β E,A,\alpha,B,\beta are fit by optimizing the Huber loss ( δ = 10 − 3 \delta=10^{-3} ) on log ⁡ L \log L with L-BFGS-B. We fit scaling laws for Scratch , SZP , and Net2Net in both LLM and MLP settings. Appendix H.2 reports the parameters and R 2 R^{2} values, all above 0.99 0.99 , confirming fit quality. In Figure 5 , we visualize the difference in modeled loss between WS methods and Scratch fits as Isolines (contour lines of equal loss difference), marking the zero-difference contour in green as the boundary for our analysis. First, the existence of this boundary across MLPs and LLMs indicates regimes where training from Scratch can be preferred over WS . Second, the boundary’s position relative to the Chinchilla-optimal tokens/parameter front (solid black line) suggests that training for fewer tokens/parameter is more likely to retain WS gains. Importantly, this bound is predictive, subject to the quality of the fits. These scaling-law fits and Iso-Loss Difference contours provide a wider picture that corroborates our initial hypothesis on the necessity of function-preservation for WS . In the MLP setup, Net2Net provides a clear front of WS gains with stronger final performance than Scratch . This is an expected result, as function-preservation was designed for MLPs. However, SZP provides a larger range of WS efficacy, with the loss-difference front pushed further from the Chinchilla-optimal front. As a contrasting case, for LLMs we observe that Net2Net shows only a small region of predicted gains over Scratch , consistent with the trends in Figure 4 . For LLMs, SZP offers a reasonable front, indicating scaling trends for when WS becomes worse than Scratch training. In summary , shorter training budgets ( ≤ 20 ​ tokens/parameter \leq 20~\textit{tokens/parameter}{} ) are more likely to yield WS gains over Scratch . For fair comparison of WS operations, the scaling pattern must be assessed and the front beyond which WS loses its advantage characterized, yielding prescriptive and predictive guidance.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We have characterized the upper bound on the growth factor within which Warmstarting ( WS ) remains computationally advantageous over training from Scratch . Beyond g upper g_{\text{upper}} , efficiency gains diminish significantly. Our analysis reveals that this limit is fundamentally tied to the training budget. We distill our contributions into a set of principled guidelines for the community: ∙ \bullet Model Scaling: If only one model run is feasible, g = 2 g=2 is the most reliable scaling for WS . ∙ \bullet Efficiency Window: WS should be prioritized over Scratch when training at or below compute-optimal scaling ( 20 20 tokens/parameter ). ∙ \bullet LR Transfer: μ ​ P \mu\text{P} serves as a principled strategy for hyperparameter transfer in WS , particularly when tuning budgets for larger scales are constrained. ∙ \bullet Standardized Reporting: We propose future WS literature explicitly report the empirical g upper g_{\text{upper}} wherever possible, and that comparisons account for scaling patterns of diminishing WS gains. We show that SZP ( Shrink-Zero-Perturb ), which augments zero-padding with a shrink-and-perturb strategy, is architecture-agnostic and more broadly applicable than function-preserving methods. SZP is easier to interpret, control, and study across architectures and setups, and our work here offers future WS literature both a framework to assess limits and make fairer comparisons of WS operations.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our empirical study is constrained by the computational costs of language model training and the need for controlled comparisons. To reflect realistic scenarios where only model checkpoints are available, we treat the base model as a black box regarding its training history. While this distinguishes our work from studies that assume full access to base training compute ( Liew and Kato, 2025 ) , it limits our ability to analyze the joint compute-optimal frontier across base size, target size, and tokens invested in both training phases. However, our findings at sub- 1 1 B scales align with trends reported at 1 1 B+ scales in prior work, suggesting transferability to larger regimes. Additionally, exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps across all growth operators remain computationally prohibitive at the language model scale. Our comparison focuses on SZP vs. Net2Net to establish a representative baseline, with the understanding that SZP can serve as a modular alternative for width-scaling methods extending Net2Net . Especially, combining with depth-scaling ( Du et al., 2024 ) for jointly growing both depth and width.

sections.heading: Future Directions.
sections.text: Several promising avenues emerge from this work. First, benchmarking SZP across diverse architectures and data modalities would validate its generality beyond language models. Second, understanding the individual contributions of shrinking and perturbation within shrink-and-perturb could reveal whether these components can be predictively scaled using fixed rules or scaling law fits, and extending to WS of optimizers too. Third, given the existence of upper bounds on growth factors, exploring progressive growing and optimal growth schedules becomes a natural next step. Fourth, extending the scaling law to jointly model loss as a function of parameters, tokens, and growth factor would remove the need to fix the growth factor across experiments, enabling predictions for arbitrary growth factors from a single unified fit. More broadly, as specialized model checkpoints become increasingly available, strengthening the practical impact of warmstarting methods will be critical for improving resource efficiency across the field.

sections.heading: Appendix A Supporting Related Work
sections.text: Scaled parameterizations refer to a set of rules that determine how certain parameters can be scaled with respect to one or more scaling dimensions [ Everett et al., 2024 ] . This family of parameterizations describes scaling factors for the weights, the learning rate, and the standard deviation of the initialization. Each of these scaling variables can be defined separately for the input, hidden, and output layers (see Tables 1, 2, 3 3 3 3 and the μ ​ P \mu\text{P}{} Github page: https://github.com/microsoft/mup/blob/main/README.md in Yang and Hu [2021] ). The maximal update parameterization or μ ​ P \mu\text{P}{} is one such parameterization that showed its scaling rules to allow for stable training of larger networks without requiring re-tuning of the variables (such as learning rate) being scaled [ Yang et al., 2021 ] , i.e., feature learning does occur at infinite-width scaling [ Yang and Hu, 2021 ] , extending the Neural Tangent Kernel [ Jacot et al., 2018 ] theory demonstrating lazy-training (fixed features) when the network is scaled to infinite-width. Follow-up works exploited the symmetry in these parameterizations to provide alternative scaling rules [ Blake et al., 2025 ] , extended to meta learning [ Thérien et al., 2024 ] , and applied to newer optimizers [ Essential AI et al., 2025 ] . Generally, in practice, a network where the learning rate is adequately tuned on a small-width network can be scaled using μ ​ P \mu\text{P}{} to be used as the learning rate for a larger width (theoretically, ∞ \infty -width), and still exhibit stable training dynamics (no blowup of L1 norms of pre-activations or output logits). While μ \mu P does not inherently predict loss values, its ability to preserve feature learning remains effective across diverse empirical settings [ Vyas et al., 2023 ] . Consequently, hyperparameter transfer is well-aligned with the predictable loss trajectories observed in language model training [ Dey et al., 2024 , Bjorck et al., 2025 ] . Scaling laws formalize these trajectories by deriving parametric power-law fits of optimal loss against compute, dataset size, or parameter count [ Kaplan et al., 2020 , Hoffmann et al., 2022 , Sorscher et al., 2022 , Alabdulmohsin et al., 2023 , Caballero et al., 2023 ] . Given a pretraining dataset and model architecture type, multiple models are trained varying the number of tokens seen, the model hyperparameters (including batch size), and the model sizes (width-depth). The resulting Pareto front characterizes the loss-compute trade-off, which is approximately linear on log-log axes and is commonly modeled with a power-law fit. This fit can then be used to predict the tokens required for compute-optimal loss given a fixed model, or the model size required for compute-optimal loss given a fixed token set to process. Chinchilla [ Hoffmann et al., 2022 ] notably showed that this fit is sensitive to the hyperparameter choices, e.g., the length of cosine decay in the learning rate schedule. Subsequent works have looked at such a role of hyperparameters when scaling models [ Porian et al., 2024 ] , and also the suitability of certain hyperparameters to allow for compute reuse while scaling [ Hägele et al., 2024 ] . Often, the role of optimal hyperparameters is highlighted as crucial but inadequately reported. Hyperparameter transfer methods become a key ingredient of a scaling recipe, and also influence novel observations for the scaling regime, such as scaling collapse [ Qiu et al., 2025 ] . Bergsma et al. [2025] look at how μ ​ P \mu\text{P} , collapsed scaling curves, and novel parametric forms for scaling relationships together can be leveraged for early stopping learning curves.

sections.heading: B.4 Details on μ ​ Parameterization \mu\text{Parameterization}
sections.text: Changing the width of a neural network changes not only its parameter count, but also the effective scale of activations, gradients, logits, and parameter updates. Therefore, hyperparameters tuned at one width need not transfer reliably to another. This creates a practical confounder for WS experiments: if each target width is retuned independently, improvements may come from better target-scale hyperparameters rather than from the growth operator itself. μ ​ Parameterization \mu\text{Parameterization} [ Yang et al., 2021 ] addresses this issue by prescribing width-dependent initialization and learning-rate scalings. Its goal is to keep models of different widths in a comparable feature-learning regime, so that the effect of parameter updates on activations remains stable as width changes. Equivalently, μ ​ P \mu\text{P}{} can be viewed as a hyperparameter-transfer rule from a small base model to a larger target model. Given a base-width configuration h n 0 = ( η , λ wd , B , w warmup , w cooldown , … ) , h_{n_{0}}=(\eta,\lambda_{\mathrm{wd}},B,w_{\mathrm{warmup}},w_{\mathrm{cooldown}},\ldots), we obtain the target-width configuration by h n = T μ ​ P ​ ( h n 0 , n 0 , n ) , h_{n}=T_{\mu\text{P}}(h_{n_{0}};n_{0},n), where T μ ​ P T_{\mu\text{P}{}} applies parameter-type-specific scaling rules to initialization and optimizer hyperparameters. The main rules are summarized in Table 3 . The key point is that different tensors can have different width dependencies: input weights, hidden weights, readout weights, embeddings, normalization parameters, and attention-logit scaling are not all treated in the same way. In practice, we specify base shapes for the model, identify which dimensions grow with width, and apply the corresponding μ ​ P \mu\text{P}{} optimizer rules. We use μ ​ P \mu\text{P}{} only as a practical mechanism for hyperparameter transfer. In the synthetic MLP benchmark, we can compare it directly against dense target-width tuning and against static transfer , where the best base-width hyperparameters are reused unchanged. sections.heading: Appendix C Design Intuition and Ablations for SZP
sections.text: This appendix complements the empirical setup in Section 4.1 by analyzing the main design choices in SZP . The method combines three simple ingredients: zero-padding, perturbation, and shrinkage. Zero-padding embeds the trained base model into the larger model, perturbation activates the newly added parameters, and shrinkage reduces the dominance of the copied base-model path. We first give a simple theoretical intuition for these roles, then provide a mechanistic interpretability analysis of their effect on weight statistics during training, and finally ablate the two nontrivial design choices: the perturbation scale and the shrinkage factor.

sections.heading: Zero-padding as an Exact Embedding.
sections.text: Consider a feed-forward network with hidden states h ℓ + 1 = ϕ ⁡ ( W ℓ ​ h ℓ + b ℓ ) , h_{\ell+1}=\phi(W_{\ell}h_{\ell}+b_{\ell}), where ϕ ⁡ ( 0 ) = 0 \phi(0)=0 . Let P ⁡ ( θ ) P(\theta) denote the width expansion from width n n to width m > n m>n by adding new neurons and setting every parameter touching them to zero. If we embed each hidden state as h ~ ℓ = [ h ℓ 0 ] , \tilde{h}_{\ell}=\begin{bmatrix}h_{\ell}\\ 0\end{bmatrix}, then the widened layer acts as h ~ ℓ + 1 = ϕ ⁡ ( [ W ℓ 0 0 0 ] ​ [ h ℓ 0 ] + [ b ℓ 0 ] ) = [ ϕ ⁡ ( W ℓ ​ h ℓ + b ℓ ) 0 ] = [ h ℓ + 1 0 ] . \tilde{h}_{\ell+1}=\phi\!\left(\begin{bmatrix}W_{\ell}&0\\ 0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}h_{\ell}\\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}b_{\ell}\\ 0\end{bmatrix}\right)=\begin{bmatrix}\phi(W_{\ell}h_{\ell}+b_{\ell})\\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}h_{\ell+1}\\ 0\end{bmatrix}. By induction over layers, F P ⁡ ( θ ) ​ ( x ) = f θ ​ ( x ) for all ​ x . F_{P(\theta)}(x)=f_{\theta}(x)\qquad\text{for all }x. Thus, in this idealized unnormalized setting, zero-padding preserves the pretrained function exactly. For normalized architectures such as Transformers with LayerNorm or RMSNorm, exact function preservation may additionally require coordinated rescaling of normalization parameters or adjacent weights – without this, zero-padding should be viewed as an embedding intuition rather than a strict function-preserving operation. However, this exact embedding is also restrictive. Let ℳ := { P ⁡ ( θ ) : θ ∈ Θ small } \mathcal{M}:=\{P(\theta):\theta\in\Theta_{\mathrm{small}}\} be the embedded small-model manifold. At points in ℳ \mathcal{M} , each newly added neuron has zero activation and zero outgoing weight. By the chain rule of backpropagation, because the outgoing weights are exactly zero, the error signal propagated back to these new neurons is zero. Consequently, the gradients with respect to all newly added parameters vanish, and under standard gradient descent, ∇ Θ new ℒ ​ ( P ⁡ ( θ ) ) = 0 . \nabla_{\Theta_{\mathrm{new}}}\mathcal{L}(P(\theta))=0. Thus, pure zero-padding can keep optimization on the embedded small-model manifold, preventing the wider model from using its additional capacity.

sections.text: The SZP initialization can be written as Θ 0 = λ shrink ​ P ​ ( θ ⋆ ) + E , 0 < λ shrink ≤ 1 , \Theta_{0}=\lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}P(\theta^{\star})+E,\qquad 0<\lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}\leq 1, where θ ⋆ \theta^{\star} is the pretrained base-model solution and E E is a perturbation. For one widened layer, partition old and new coordinates and write the input as h ~ = [ h h new ] , \tilde{h}=\begin{bmatrix}h\\ h_{\mathrm{new}}\end{bmatrix}, where h new = 0 h_{\mathrm{new}}=0 for pure zero-padding and h new = O ⁡ ( ‖ E ‖ ) h_{\mathrm{new}}=O(\|E\|) after perturbations from preceding layers. The following calculation keeps only first-order terms in the perturbation magnitude. Let the perturbation matrix and bias vector be conformably partitioned into blocks corresponding to the old (o) and new (n) dimensions: E = [ E o ​ o E o ​ n E n ​ o E n ​ n ] , e = [ e o e n ] . E=\begin{bmatrix}E_{oo}&E_{on}\\ E_{no}&E_{nn}\end{bmatrix},\qquad e=\begin{bmatrix}e_{o}\\ e_{n}\end{bmatrix}. The preactivation then takes the form z ~ = [ λ shrink ​ ( W ​ h + b ) 0 ] + [ E o ​ o ​ h + e o E n ​ o ​ h + e n ] + O ⁡ ( ‖ E ‖ 2 ) . \tilde{z}=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}(Wh+b)\\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}E_{oo}h+e_{o}\\ E_{no}h+e_{n}\end{bmatrix}+O(\|E\|^{2}). The lower block, E n ​ o ​ h + e n , E_{no}h+e_{n}, is the first nonzero signal available to the newly added neurons. If E = 0 E=0 , the new coordinates remain inactive. Thus, perturbation moves the model off the embedded manifold ℳ \mathcal{M} and activates the added degrees of freedom. Shrinkage plays a complementary role. It reduces the copied old-path signal from ‖ W ​ h + b ‖ \|Wh+b\| to approximately λ shrink ​ ‖ W ​ h + b ‖ \lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}\|Wh+b\| , while the new-path signal remains controlled by the perturbation. The relative influence of the new coordinates is therefore, to first order, ‖ ( z ~ ) new ‖ ‖ ( z ~ ) old ‖ = ‖ E n ​ o ​ h + e n + O ⁡ ( ‖ E ‖ 2 ) ‖ ‖ λ shrink ​ ( W ​ h + b ) + E o ​ o ​ h + e o + O ⁡ ( ‖ E ‖ 2 ) ‖ . \frac{\|(\tilde{z})_{\mathrm{new}}\|}{\|(\tilde{z})_{\mathrm{old}}\|}=\frac{\|E_{no}h+e_{n}+O(\|E\|^{2})\|}{\|\lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}(Wh+b)+E_{oo}h+e_{o}+O(\|E\|^{2})\|}. When the copied old-path signal dominates the old-block perturbation, i.e., λ shrink ​ ‖ W ​ h + b ‖ ≫ ‖ E o ​ o ​ h + e o ‖ , \lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}\|Wh+b\|\gg\|E_{oo}h+e_{o}\|, this simplifies to ‖ ( z ~ ) new ‖ ‖ ( z ~ ) old ‖ ≈ ‖ E n ​ o ​ h + e n ‖ λ shrink ​ ‖ W ​ h + b ‖ . \frac{\|(\tilde{z})_{\mathrm{new}}\|}{\|(\tilde{z})_{\mathrm{old}}\|}\approx\frac{\|E_{no}h+e_{n}\|}{\lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}\|Wh+b\|}. Taking λ shrink < 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}<1 makes it easier for the newly added neurons to compete with the copied subnetwork. Crucially, a larger relative preactivation ensures that the newly added weights generate correspondingly larger gradients during backpropagation, actively pulling the optimization trajectory away from the restrictive manifold ℳ \mathcal{M} . In summary, zero-padding preserves the pretrained model, perturbation activates the new dimensions, and shrinkage accelerates adaptation by breaking the optimization dominance of the inherited narrow solution.

sections.heading: C.4 Shrinkage Ablation
sections.text: Shrinkage controls the strength of the copied base-model path in SZP . In the initialization Θ 0 = λ shrink ​ P ​ ( θ ⋆ ) + E \Theta_{0}=\lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}P(\theta^{\star})+E , smaller values of λ shrink \lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}} reduce the contribution of the inherited narrow solution, while the perturbation E E activates the newly added coordinates. As discussed in Section C.1 , this makes it easier for the new neurons to compete with the copied subnetwork after growth. This role of shrinkage is consistent with recent work on plasticity in warm-started networks. DASH [ Shin et al., 2024 ] also uses shrinkage to mitigate plasticity loss, but does so in a direction-aware manner: weights associated with useful learned features are preserved more strongly, while components attributed to memorized noise are shrunk more aggressively. In contrast, SZP intentionally uses a single global shrinkage factor, making it architecture-agnostic and easy to combine with arbitrary growth operators. Relatedly, weight clipping has been proposed as a simple way to control weight magnitudes and improve plasticity in continual and reinforcement learning settings [ Elsayed et al., 2024 ] . Our use of shrinkage can be viewed as a one-shot initialization-time analogue of this broader norm-control principle. We ablate λ shrink \lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}} while keeping the remaining SZP settings fixed. Figure 9 reports final validation loss across three base checkpoints, three token budgets, and multiple target scales. Across settings, the best values are concentrated in the low-to-moderate shrinkage regime, typically around λ shrink ∈ { 0.2 , 0.4 } \lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}\in\{0.2,0.4\} . Setting λ shrink \lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}} too close to 1 1 corresponds to little or no shrinkage, leaving the grown model more dominated by the inherited base-model path. Conversely, setting it too close to 0 0 removes too much of the pretrained signal and makes the initialization closer to perturbation-only growth. The broad minimum around 0.2 0.2 – 0.4 0.4 suggests that shrinkage is useful, but does not require precise tuning. We use λ shrink = 0.4 \lambda_{\mathrm{shrink}}=0.4 in the main experiments as a stable default in this low-loss region. This choice is also consistent with the post-hoc analysis in Figure 7 : compared with perturbation alone, adding shrinkage improves effective rank and permits larger movement from initialization, indicating that the grown model better uses its added capacity rather than remaining anchored to the base model. Equivalently, this form of width-scaling adds more heads of the same size to each layer. This approach is standard in the literature, especially when studying feature learning under width-scaling [ Everett et al., 2024 ] . We note that this form of width-scaling provides the fairest setup for comparing WS methods. The query , key , and value weights are grouped per head within a tensor. For a simple mental illustration, a 1 1 -head network with width 1 1 will have an attention tensor with 3 3 dimensions, one each for query , key , and value , assuming no weight sharing. When grown to width 2 2 by scaling the head dimension, the flattened attention tensor has 6 6 dimensions, 2 2 each for query , key , and value . This introduces a subtle layout inefficiency: under index-wise growth, the second dimension of the query block in the larger model corresponds to the key dimension of the smaller model. This correspondence is maintained cleanly when width-scaling is implemented by increasing only the number of heads while keeping the head size fixed.

sections.heading: Appendix G Net2Net
sections.text: Net2Net [ Chen et al., 2016 ] is a seminal function-preserving growth method: it expands a trained base network into a larger target network by duplicating/splitting hidden units (width) and/or inserting identity layers (depth), such that the target initially computes (approximately) the same function as the base. In recent standardized evaluations of model growth for LLM pre-training, a Net2Net -style direct width-expansion operator is used as the canonical function-preserving width-growth baseline (often referred to as a “direct” growth operator) [ Du et al., 2024 ] . We therefore adopt Net2Net as our primary width warmstarting baseline.

sections.heading: G.1 Why Net2Net?
sections.text: We use Net2Net [ Chen et al., 2016 ] because it (1) targets width expansion , which is the focus of this work, (2) is (approximately) function-preserving at initialization, and (3) requires no changes to the training objective or additional optimization stages. This makes it a clean and widely used baseline for isolating the effect of the warmstarted initialization. Moreover, in the large-scale growth benchmark of Du et al. [2024] , the Net2Net-style direct widening operator is the strongest width-expansion baseline among the compared growth operators, motivating its use as our primary width warmstarting baseline.

sections.heading: Why not other Methods?
sections.text: We exclude several alternative strategies by design. Learned growth and distillation-based methods (for example, linear transformations [ Wang et al., 2023a ] , progressive module training [ Gong et al., 2019 ] , or teacher–student frameworks [ Qin et al., 2021 ] ) introduce additional stages (e.g., auxiliary alignment losses or intermediate supervision), which makes it harder to attribute gains specifically to initialization quality. Importantly, our method could be composed with such techniques; however, such extensions are outside the scope of this work.

sections.heading: Intuition.
sections.text: Width growth in Net2Net can be viewed as splitting a hidden unit into several identical copies, then rescaling the outgoing weights so that the combined contribution of the copies matches the original unit. Figure 12 illustrates this matrix-level perspective: we first expand the input dimension (duplicate columns), then expand the output dimension (duplicate rows). Figure 12: Net2Net-style matrix expansion. A width expansion can be implemented by duplicating columns (fan-in growth) and rows (fan-out growth), corresponding to adding new hidden units (highlighted). We use this figure (adapted from transformer growth descriptions building on Net2Net and bert2BERT ) to illustrate the operation. Sourced from [ Chen et al., 2021 ] .

sections.text: The same idea can be written compactly at the matrix level. For a linear map W ∈ ℝ d out × d in W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}} expanded to W ′ ∈ ℝ D out × D in W^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\text{out}}\times D_{\text{in}}} , Net2Net-style widening can be expressed as W ′ = L ​ W ​ R , W^{\prime}=L\,W\,R, (8) where R R duplicates (copies) input dimensions, i.e., columns of W W , to reach D in D_{\text{in}} , and L L duplicates output dimensions, i.e., rows of W W , to reach D out D_{\text{out}} . To preserve the function, L L and/or R R additionally include a 1 / c 1/c rescaling for duplicated units, where c c is the copy count of the corresponding source unit. This is the same “copy-and-rescale” operator view commonly used when describing width growth in transformer blocks [ Du et al., 2024 ] .

sections.heading: Noise for Symmetry Breaking.
sections.text: Because duplicated units start identically, we optionally add small Gaussian noise to the newly created parameters (or to a subset of duplicated rows/columns) to break symmetry, following standard Net2Net practice [ Chen et al., 2016 ] . In our experiments this noise is small enough to keep the initialization close to function-preserving while avoiding perfectly identical copies.

sections.heading: MLPs.
sections.text: In the synthetic MLP experiments, we apply the widening rule above to each hidden layer: we duplicate hidden units according to π \pi and rescale the corresponding outgoing weights by the copy counts, optionally injecting small Gaussian noise for symmetry breaking.

sections.heading: Transformers.
sections.text: In the transformer language-model experiments, we apply the same function-preserving principle when expanding width. Concretely, we grow matrices whose inner dimensions scale with model width (e.g., token embeddings and the projection matrices in attention/MLP blocks) via the same “copy columns / copy rows + rescale” recipe in Equation 8 . For multi-head attention, because we keep the head size fixed and grow width by adding heads, copying is performed at the level of complete heads: duplicated W q W_{q} , W k W_{k} , and W v W_{v} rows are left unscaled, while the copy-count rescaling is applied only to the corresponding W o W_{o} columns. This preserves the duplicated heads’ softmax computation while averaging their combined contribution through the output projection. This yields an initialization that matches the base model computation as closely as possible at the moment of expansion, while remaining a drop-in replacement that does not modify the objective or training loop. All comparisons use identical token budgets and optimization settings to isolate the effect of initialization.

sections.heading: G.4 Scope and Follow-up Work
sections.text: While our study focuses on width-only growth, Net2Net [ Chen et al., 2016 ] also proposes depth-expanding transformations (e.g., inserting identity layers). In transformers, bert2BERT [ Chen et al., 2021 ] extends Net2Net -style ideas to BERT, and combines them with layer stacking to grow depth. More broadly, depth expansion can be paired with transformer-specific stacking strategies, such as those explored in Stacking Your Transformers [ Du et al., 2024 ] . Our empirical study isolates width scaling (following Everett et al. [2024] ) because our emphasis on hyperparameter transfer and scaling behavior requires extensive sweeps across widths, training horizons, and transfer settings. Nevertheless, extending our warmstarting analysis to depth is a natural next step, and should be compatible with depth-stacking mechanisms and depth-aware scaling rules (e.g., depth μ ​ P \mu\text{P} variants and recipe-based transfers such as completeP [ Dey et al., 2025 ] ). Ultimately, this points toward studying warmstarting under compound scaling; we first establish controlled evidence for hyperparameter transfer under width growth [ Everett et al., 2024 , Dey et al., 2025 , Essential AI et al., 2025 ] .

sections.heading: Further Applications.
sections.text: So far, we have used scaling-law fits to characterize when warmstarting is effective compared with training from scratch. The same approach can also be used for comparing Warmstarting methods against each other. In Figure 18 , we compare SZP and Net2Net by plotting isolines of the difference between their fitted loss surfaces across model sizes and training budgets. In the LLM setting, SZP is predicted to outperform Net2Net across all configurations. In the MLP setting, Net2Net is competitive at low token budgets, where its function-preservation properties are most beneficial, but SZP is predicted to perform better at larger token budgets. This aligns with the design of each method: Net2Net preserves the base model’s function, providing an immediate advantage, while SZP enables the use of new neurons (see Section C.2 ), which becomes increasingly beneficial as the training budget grows and the model has more room to adapt. More broadly, this demonstrates that scaling law fits enable a richer comparison between warmstarting methods than evaluations at a single training budget, capturing how each method’s effectiveness varies with both model size and training duration. Neeratyoy Mallik 1,2,∗ Maciej Janowski 1,3,∗ Johannes Hog 1,∗ Herilalaina Rakotoarison 4 Josif Grabocka 3 Frank Hutter 5,6,1 Aaron Klein 6 1 University of Freiburg 2 Zuse School ELIZA 3 University of Technology Nuremberg 4 University of Helsinki 5 Prior Labs 6 ELLIS Institute Tübingen * Equal contribution. Correspondence: {mallik,janowski,hogj}@cs.uni-freiburg.de Abstract Model growth from a given checkpoint aims to accelerate training of a larger model, offering potential resource savings. Despite recent interest, warmstarting has seen limited practical adoption in large-scale training. We attribute this to two underexplored factors: (1) an overemphasis on preserving the smaller model’s performance at initialization, which constrains operator design for new architectures, and (2) insufficient analysis of how growth interacts with hyperparameters and scaling behavior, compounded by inconsistent growth factors across the literature. We show that preserving the base model’s initial post-growth performance is not necessary for strong final performance, and that simple, architecture-agnostic growth strategies can outperform more complex warmstarting operators. Crucially, we empirically identify an upper bound on the growth factor g g beyond which training from scratch is more efficient. We observe this across multiple ablation setups. Notably, this limit is also present, but unreported, in prior published results. Across our experiments on dense MLPs and dense language models, we find that a 2 × 2\times growth factor is the most reliable in yielding convergence speedups, with gains most pronounced under 20 tokens/parameter budgets and diminishing as budget increases. We fit scaling laws over these observations to provide predictive guidance for practitioners deciding when and how much to grow. Together, our analysis provides practical guidelines and empirical limits for model growth. 1 Introduction Training state-of-the-art deep learning models requires significant computational resources. As models scale from millions to billions of parameters, practitioners face an important question: can we reuse the compute invested in training smaller models when scaling up? Model growth or warmstarting ( WS ), i.e., initializing larger models from trained smaller checkpoints, offers potential efficiency gains, yet remains largely absent from production pipelines despite substantial research ( Gong et al., 2019 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Rae et al., 2021 ; Shen et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023a ; Wang et al., 2023b ; Deng et al., 2023 ; Samragh et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Deep Learning (DL) success has been built on pushing the loss frontier across tasks, applications, and data modalities ( Krizhevsky et al., 2012 ; He et al., 2016 ; Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Brown et al., 2020 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; OpenAI, 2024 ) . As training efficacy improves, processing larger datasets drives corresponding increases in model capacity ( Alabdulmohsin et al., 2023 ) . Current research on frontier models builds on seminal scaling law studies demonstrating the necessity of simultaneously growing both model size and data processed ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . This co-scaling question continues to evolve across different constraints, modalities, and architectures, with the traditional goal of pushing the loss-frontier now complemented by optimizing the compute-optimal frontier ( Anagnostidis et al., 2024 ) . In practice, these considerations translate to decisions about resource efficiency ( Wan et al., 2023 ) . While WS has been periodically explored across architectures and paradigms, it has not become standard practice in training pipelines, often remaining an academic topic rather than a common choice in DL pipelines ( Gong et al., 2019 ; Wang et al., 2023a ) . We identify three barriers to practical WS adoption: 1) Implementation complexity: existing methods require architecture-specific adaptations and may not generalize to modern components ( Su et al., 2021 ; Gu and Dao, 2023 ) ; 2) Unclear growth limits: practitioners lack guidance on how much a given checkpoint can be grown before WS becomes counterproductive ( Xie et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023a ) ; 3) Hyperparameter opacity under scaling: the interaction between WS methods, hyperparameters, and model and data scaling budgets is under-explored, creating tuning overhead that undermines efficiency gains ( Fetterman et al., 2023 ; Dey et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, in scaling regimes where both models and data grow to improve final convergence loss, measuring relative early-stage convergence speed may not adequately capture practical requirements ( Shin et al., 2024 ; Unlu, 2026 ) . In this work, we attempt to systematically investigate when WS is truly effective, in a first-principles manner, to address these barriers. We limit the discussion scope, both for clarity and computation, for the case when a base model checkpoint is available to be WS -ed to a larger model scale. We assume that we are aware of the dataset the base was trained on, and that some of its training hyperparameters may be available, but we treat it as a black-box when it comes to the training compute invested in it (unlike the assumption made by Liew and Kato (2025) ). We believe this better reflects a real-world scenario where only model checkpoints are publicly released. Our contributions are: 1. We generalize warmstarting growth into shrink-zero-perturb ( SZP ), a simple architecture-agnostic operation, and find that exact function-preservation is not required for effective warmstarting. 2. We empirically establish an upper bound on the growth ratio of a given checkpoint, such that, beyond this bound, training the grown model from scratch converges as fast as warmstarting it. 3. We release our model and training pipelines in the linked repository 1 1 1 https://github.com/Neeratyoy/warmstarting_exps . 2 Related Works Model growth as initialization is the broad class of WS techniques that derive the weights of a larger model from a smaller, typically well-trained checkpoint, before beginning training. Here, the aim is to transfer the knowledge learned by the smaller model to improve the larger model’s training efficiency. Net2Net ( Chen et al., 2016 ) and Network Morphisms ( Wei et al., 2016 ) are among the earliest works exploring model growth for Deep Learning. At the time, the scope was limited to convolutional networks, but the core idea was carried forward to evolving architectures ( Gong et al., 2019 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Samragh et al., 2024 ) . The benefit lies in being a one-time operation before training, requiring only weights from a smaller network of the same architectural family. A central idea in designing WS operations for initialization is that of function-preservation ( FP ), wherein the grown model’s output at the first forward pass matches that of the base model checkpoint used for WS . Introduced by Chen et al. (2016) for Deep Learning, FP has dominated the width-scaling WS paradigm ( Wang et al., 2023b ; Samragh et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . However, with new architectures, it typically requires special adaptation to remain function preserving ( Chen et al., 2021 ; Samragh et al., 2024 ) . We thus question if FP at initialization is a requirement for model growth. Karp et al. (2024) already showed that loss after a short training budget correlates better than loss at initialization with growth operator rankings. We extend this to more practical training budgets. Learned model growth is the other family of WS that does not fix the exact manner of WS operation but handles it dynamically. Wang et al. (2023a) introduces a Kronecker-factored linear operator that parameterizes the linear map from the small to the larger model, learned over a few steps of training (in the style of Karp et al. (2024) ). Here, the Kronecker product constrains growth ratios but works for both width and depth. Evci et al. (2022) looks at dynamic model growing during training by maximizing the gradient norms of the newly added neurons to enforce faster convergence, while the output-preservation in the function-preservation -style is still implied. The learned component here comes from the newly grown weights set through SVD over the gradient on the activations. This design looks to prevent dead neurons in grown models, which can lead to early rank collapse or not utilize the grown parameter capacity and move sufficiently away in the function hypothesis space from the base model. This connects to plasticity loss ( Lyle et al., 2023 ) , which correlates with dead (inactive) neurons, low effective rank representations, and growing weight magnitudes. Dohare et al. (2023) addresses this for a trained model by selectively reinitializing a fraction of low-utility neurons, scored by their activations, after each training step to keep a model in a continual learning setup. In this work, we focus entirely on the more straightforward setup of initialization-only WS . Full-state Warmstarting looks beyond the weights. Wang et al. (2024) looks at the learning rate schedulers, Ma et al. (2026) and Yu et al. (2026) necessitate the WS of optimizer states too. These families aim to preserve loss (and thereby FP ), while suitably inducing training dynamics through optimizer schedules and states, including hyperparameters. Our setup assumes that only the smaller model checkpoint is available and no other information on the optimizer or scheduler, especially their states. The framework of investigation we offer in our paper should apply to future studies extending to complete training state warmstarts, too. Warmstarting in practical settings has been covered mostly in terms of operator selection ( Karp et al., 2024 ) , for scaling related recommendations involving scaling laws ( Wang et al., 2023b ; Liew and Kato, 2025 ) , and the role of width-depth in WS efficacy ( Du et al., 2024 ) . We note that most WS literature varies in their setups, especially with respect to growth factors g g (the ratio of target to base model parameters) and the budget involved in training. Our investigation in this work focuses specifically on width-scaling strategies. Typically, joint scaling of models along both dimensions requires independent choice of width- and depth-growth operators ( Du et al., 2024 ) . Our study here is compatible with any depth-growing and thereby joint-growing setups. We adopt a “black-box” assumption where the tokens spent on the base checkpoint are unknown, and we are concerned primarily with the question of how much we can grow this model, by training for how much budget, to ensure there is a benefit over training from scratch. In the remaining paper, we treat the terms Model Growth and Warmstarting ( WS ) synonymously. We first introduce a compact design space for growth ( Section 3.1 ) that abstracts common warmstarting operators. We then use this space to identify a robust, architecture-agnostic default in SZP ( Section 3.2 ). 3.1 Design Space for Warmstarting To study when Warmstarting is effective, we compare simple, architecture-agnostic WS operations against training from scratch. Function-preservation ( FP ) methods typically combine three ingredients: cloning existing weights, scaling grown weights, and adding noise, often through architecture-specific rules ( Chen et al., 2016 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Samragh et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) (see Appendix G ). We instead keep these interacting design choices independent and apply them uniformly across all components, both 1 1 D and 2 2 D weights. We define our design space by extending the shrink-and-perturb ( SnP ) formulation from Continual Learning (CL) ( Ash and Adams, 2020 ) . By separating 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , λ shrink \lambda_{\text{shrink}}{} , and σ perturb \sigma_{\text{perturb}}{} in a WS operations, it gives a lightweight abstraction of common FP -style operations without requiring component-specific rules for exact function preservation. Conceptually, Growth determines which structure is inherited from the base model. Perturbation is critical for symmetry breaking, that is, it ensures that newly added neurons can learn distinct features rather than simply duplicating inherited behavior. Finally, Shrinking reduces the magnitude of inherited weights, dampening the dominance of base representations, and allows the new neurons to participate meaningfully in learning. Together, these axes yield simple WS realizations that connect cleanly to established CL concepts while remaining easy to implement. While simplicity is subjective, SZP strikes a practical middle ground: it mirrors the structure of standard FP algorithms while loosening the strict constraint of preserving base-model outputs at initialization. We emphasize that SZP is not proposed as a new state-of-the-art warmstarting algorithm, but as a principled baseline we find effective for studying the scaling behavior of WS in Section 4 . 4 Empirical Study In this section, we use the SZP setup to study its scaling behavior, compare against popular function-preservation baselines such as Net2Net , observe the existence of an upper bound on the growth factor, and fit scaling laws to characterize when training from scratch outperforms Warmstarting ( WS ). The Bounded Effective Growth Factor. For practitioners with a fixed base checkpoint seeking to scale up (as scoped in Section 1 ), a key question is how much the model can grow while preserving WS ’s efficiency gains over Scratch . Prior work ( Du et al., 2024 ) shows that WS performance depends on the growth factor g g , defined as the ratio of target to base model parameters, and characterizes this via the optimal growth factor. This optimal factor, which we term g opt g_{\text{opt}} , is estimated by fitting quadratic models to IsoFLOP losses and minimizing them. g opt g_{\text{opt}} is meant to be an optimal growth factor such that it maximizes the relative gains of WS over training from Scratch . One interpretation is that Warmstarting places the target model in a region of the loss landscape shaped by the base model’s learned representations. For small g g , this initialization provides a favorable basin for efficient convergence. As g g grows, the base model occupies a diminishing fraction of the target architecture, and the initialization increasingly resembles a random one. Beyond g upper g_{\text{upper}} , the constraints imposed by the inherited structure outweigh its benefits, anchoring the warmstarted model in a suboptimal region.
